hints: Look carefully at the words less negative. Which side has the higher water potential, the surroundings outside or the cytoplasm inside the bacterium?
Remember osmosis always moves water from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential, then think about what a bacterial wall does when water enters.
walkthrough:
**Compare the two water potentials**

Think of water potential like a scale where 0 is the highest. Less negative means higher, more negative means lower.

Here: surroundings (less negative, higher) > inside cell (more negative, lower).

**Apply the osmosis rule**

Water always moves by osmosis down its water potential gradient, from higher to lower.

So water will move from the surroundings into the bacterium:
$$\text{high } \Psi \text{ (outside)} \rightarrow \text{low } \Psi \text{ (inside)}$$

**Check what the bacterial wall does**

A typical bacterium has a strong peptidoglycan cell wall outside its cell surface membrane. It is fully permeable to water but gives strength.

So water does enter, the cell becomes turgid, but the wall normally prevents it from bursting. That leaves D as the safe, correct prediction.

options.A: Water may enter, but bursting is prevented because the bacterial cell wall does have a very important structural, strengthening function.
options.B: This is the wrong direction. Water leaves only if the outside is more negative, but here the outside is less negative so water enters by osmosis.
options.C: There will be a change because the bacterial cell wall is permeable to water, it is the cell surface membrane that controls osmosis.
options.D: Correct. With higher (less negative) water potential outside, there is a net movement of water into the bacterium by osmosis.
